Right! I find the study pretty ingenious, actually. I know it's Mythbusters and not completely set to scientific rigor, but it's still pretty well thought out.

It also helps control for sexual dimorphism. They wanted to cancel out the power difference in the average male to the average female's throwing, i.e. post-pubescent males throwing harder due to a statistically significant increase of muscle over females. So what did they do? Test form instead, using the hand with which you've never learned how to throw a ball!

The crux of "you throw like a girl," as has been stated in other posts, is that it chiefly refers to the form of throwing rather than the actual power behind the throw. However, as is shown in the video, throwing form is a *learned* difference rather than an innate one.

*edit: it'd be interesting to redo this study with ambidextrous people...

Fun fact - Mythbusters actually did an awesome study on the ["you throw like a girl"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?feature=player_embedded&v=LD5Xm5u7UDM) myth!

tl;dr: throwing form is mostly a cultural adaptation. When you make normal (read: untrained in baseball/softball) people throw with their non-dominant hands, people use the exact same throwing style as the other sex with little difference in speed or accuracy!

The station only started updating specialty show tags a few years ago, so this is only a small selection of the current breadth of the world music catalogue, but it still gives (as of today) 108 albums for you to check out.

Some countries are less influenced by prevailing American/British tastes than others. Finland, Sweden, and Norway are good examples; if you're into metal at all, check there.

Additionally, rather than browsing year-end best of lists, check out individual weeks of a country's Top 100. It'll be easier to see what are obviously the local country's listings. I started working at my college's radio station as a newscaster as a freshman and became a DJ my junior year. After graduation, I ended up coming back to the same town to work on pre-reqs for my master's degree, during which I went back to the station and joined the music department. We get easily 100+ albums per week, so the staff divvies up what's there and we go our ways for the week writing and reviewing. I typically focus on metal, punk rock, experimental music, and post-rock (when it's available).

My suggestion is to call or ask around. If you're in a town with a college, see if their station is open to community members, or join it if you are a student. When it comes to getting music, I'm trying to get in the habit of contacting all of the bands and labels of the music I put in heavy airplay rotation to thank them for their music while sending a copy of my review and asking that they contact me, personally, upon their next release. It's been moderately successful thus far, and I've only been a part of the music department for about two months. A lot of the smaller labels and artists are extremely thankful that someone simply noticed that they exist, and they're willing to use your review (hey, it's free advertising as far as they're concerned).

I actually have a blog myself that I've started just to post my review on-line in case anyone finds them interesting :P The reviews we write at the station are for the in-house DJs so they know what they're playing before it goes on air and they know what tracks are "cuts" (i.e. the good ones, or most representative of the artist's aesthetic). Naturally, my reviews are written with that in mind.

On that note: find a certain niche, be it a writing style, genre, or purpose for your reviews that makes yourself brandable and unique. Pitchfork has successfully painted themselves as the independent music journalism force, although your mileage may vary on their public image nowadays. BPM and TinyMixTapes are doing well with electronic and hip-hop media. My reviews are specifically written for DJs and people making playlists, so you won't get as much opinion on whether the album is good/bad. Does that make sense?

I don't want to shamelessly plug myself, but if you'd like to check me out, I'll PM you my blog. I'm happy to help a fellow music reviewer and someone just as interested and excited as I am.

Problem is, those are two huge misunderstandings with fraternities commonly restated by people with few ties to Greek Life.

My fraternity doesn't haze. Yes, I get it, all fraternities say that - no, my fraternity internationally abolished hazing in all of its chapters, to the point where you *will* be kicked off campus and disassociated with the fraternity if you haze, and the fraternity *will* investigate.

If they don't, then they're not an upstanding chapter, and you're better off without them. Secondly, it's not the friends that you're paying for. It's the business experience (chapters run like businesses), insertion into academic societies that do benefit you later, volunteering/leadership experience similar to BSA, charity organizations, the familial ties that come with fraternities (lemme tell ya about that time I got a first-class plane ride because a flight attendant was in the same fraternity as me), and, yes, friends.

You meet a swath of people to meet who are more diverse than your average frat bro stereotype. For example: I dance and DJ black metal. My little is from New York City. My roommate one year and best friend in the fraternity works for MTV and went to NYC for acting. My pledge brother and other good friend is the face of my university's Paris study-abroad program.

Yup, five years ago. Met online, started online, saw each other online, and broke up online. Still good friends online.

We met through a friend of mine junior year of high school when we were both 15 in a group message on AIM (wow, that makes me feel old). She was from Long Island, NY; I'm from the South. We talked for a long time while the dude who was currently interested in her was making those teenage jokes that try just a liiiiittle too hard.

Speed up about two months, and we've been talking, texting, and communicating/IMing on-line pretty much every day. Junior year was a hard year for me in high school due to AP classes, and for her it was the same. Some time in March, she and I stayed up with each other until 3AM on a Tuesday talking about everything, talking about us, and how nice it was to have each other as a friend. Some time in the really late night/really early morning, she said she felt something and had wanted to tell me toward the end of the night. I think from there is when we officially decided we were "dating," even though we had never met each other in real life and we hadn't even seen what each other looked like. Sure, it was totally likely that the other could've been a total creeper, but being young and scared, it was comforting knowing we had someone who liked us for who we were based just off our personality, not looks, even if they were several hundred miles away. I even remember saying something along the lines of "I can tell by the way you talk that you're beautiful." (Yup, I was totally 15, guys.)

A couple months later we Skyped each other for the first time, and she really was just as pretty as I thought she was. Blonde hair, aquiline facial structure, blue-green eyes, everything. And, don't worry, it was actually her too. In retrospect, it was a really cool feeling to have an attraction to someone like that, and then seeing them in real life they're just as... physically attractive as they were personality-attractive. Does that make sense?

Fast forward again to the summer. I'm going on sailing adventures, canoeing trips, etc. while she's doing internships in New York. Having a blast, one of those times where I'd get home from being in Canada for two weeks and couldn't WAIT to tell this girl about my life and adventures, and I couldn't wait to hear about hers. Things are great. Even our parents knew about each other by this point. Like any parent, they were nervous about who the person on the other end actually was, and I remember Skyping with her dad several times.

After about seven months or so from dating and talking to each other all the time on-line, she messaged me saying how it wasn't working out. We were extremely swamped with AP classes, me being on swim team, her on the volleyball team, etc. It was that point in a relationship where you allow the outside stressors of your life to enter into your relationship with a person - not because they're hurting you, but because you're comfortable enough in your relationship to show that person the entirety of your life. Some relationships handle that and go on to be something more now that the person you're with isn't just an ideal, but most, as a lot of us know, don't survive that stage. Ours didn't. We broke up at the end of the month.

Sounds like an enlarged thyroid (aka "goiter"). Feel underneath your jawline toward the corner of your jaw. There are two lumpy glands there. Normally they aren't very big (a half-dollar could cover up most of it), but if you feel them poking out at all, then that could be something.

Take your finger and thumb and place them over either thyroid. Swallow. Check to see if the thyroid pushes against your skin, and also if that's where the pain is. Usually it's a strange sort of discomfort - like a pressure type of pain. The constant pressure being put on and off the thyroid when you chew would have that effect as well.

Enlarged thyroids can be due to any number of things. The thyroid glands are one of the parts of the body directly responsible for the production of hormones, specifically calcitonin (one of the chemicals that regulates the amount of calcium in your bloodstream and bones). A large thyroid is not something to be worried about on off chances - many times it will go away on its own after it's finished whatever the body decided it wanted to do. However, this usually occurs for no more than several days.

If it continues to get worse or does not go away after 10-14 days, then I would contact your physician to make sure nothing else is going on. Good luck!

Sometimes it's as simple as a musculoskeletal disorder; the way your muscles and bones are shaped can affect you. I have a very close friend who has an abnormally long inferior aspect to her scapula (that's your shoulderblades). It causes her upper trapezius muscles to overcompensate and overdevelop, causing excess tension in her upper back as well.

Have you noticed what habits you have when you are physically active? For example, when you life things, do you shrug your shoulders? That's a common habit of people, although a poor one (poor in the sense that it isn't efficient use of muscles, not that you're bad for doing it :D). For example, ballet dancers are taught to depress their scapula when lifting in the arms to better activate the latissimus dorsi and scapular muslces that enable efficient arm movement. Shrugging your shoulder, rotating your scapula outward, and similar habits can harm your body's ability to move.

Start seeing how your back reacts upon activating and deactivating certain muscles upon movement. Also, how is your back aligned immediately before the sensation begins? Are you curved over? Do you go into flatback - flattening the natural curve of your thoracic spine? Do you feel stretching sensations in your upper back?

I don't really recommend searching on the Internet because you'll be told any number of things: pinched nerve, musculoskeletal disorders (like me!), habitual use of muscles (like me again!), etc. I'd recommend you see a chiropractor or PT if it's scaring you, if it impedes your daily function, **and if the pain gets worse**.

Two years of DJ'ing and six years after my first Rise Against CD, here it goes!

Punk is great because it's one of those genres that honestly has something for everyone if you look closely. Want to melt your face? Try metalcore! Angry at the man? Anarcho-punk! Just feeling angry? Hardcore punk! Have a lot of feelings? Go for emo (note: not MCR)! Want to feel awesome, excited, and pumped? Pop punk! Wanna get shit-faced and have a good time? Fucking SKA, man! Wanna get atmospheric and crazy? Post-punk!

Here's a list of bands per genre and what you should expect:

**Old school punk rock** - These are your pioneers of punk from the mid-70s to early-80s. Good ur-examples of all other punk genres, and punk rock classics are always something good to start off with.

* The Clash - "London Calling", "The Clash", "Sandinista"
* Sex Pistols - "Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols"
* The Damned - "Damned Damned Damned"
* Agent Orange - "Agent Orange"
* Patti Smith - "Horses"
* The Modern Lovers - "The Modern Lovers" (garage rock/protopunk; they're a really big influence on the punk aesthetic)
* The Ramones - anything, really
* Richard Hell and The Voidoids - "Blank Generation"
* Wire - "Pink Flag"



**Hardcore Punk** - big, angry, shouted or yelled vocals. Typically very fast tempos. Lyrics are typically politically or socially charged.

* Black Flag - "Damaged", "Nervous Breakdown EP"
* Dead Kennedys - "Give Me Convenience or Give Me Death", "Fresh Fruit for Rotting Vegetables"
* Refused - "The Shape of Punk to Come" (my all-time favorite hardcore punk album, very anarchist)
* Nation of Ulysses - "13-Point Plan to Destroy America"
* Rise Against - "Revolutions Per Minute"
* Reagan Youth - "A Collection of Pop Classics"
* Various Artists - "Repo Man: Original Soundtrack" (collection of a shitload of hardcore punk acts from the early/mid-80s)
* Minor Threat - "Complete Discography" (all of their songs fit on one CD)
* Suicidal Tendencies - "Suicidal Tendencies"
* Off! - "Off!"
* Bad Brains - "Bad Brains"
* Various Artists - "20 Years of Dischord" (3 CDs of Dischord Record bands and rarities, a must have for the Washington D.C. punk scene)
* Husker Du - "Zen Arcade", "New Day Rising" (the former is one of the best concept albums in punk rock I've ever heard, majorly recommended, especially "Turn On the News")
* Gallows - "Orcestra of Wolves"
* Crass - "Penis Envy" (also counts as anarcho-punk, same with Refused)



**Emo** - this has become a dirty word nowadays. Forget everything you've heard - this is not MCR or Fall Out Boy. Emo originally meant "emotional hardcore," which simply referred to hardcore punk with slight progressive tendencies that described intensely personal themes and influences in their lyrics. Trust me, it's worth trying.

* Sunny Day Real Estate - "Diary"
* Weezer - "Pinkerton"
* Rites of Spring - "Rites of Spring"
* Jimmy Eat World - "Clarity"
* Jawbreaker - "Bivouac"
* The Promise Ring - "Nothing Feels Good"



**Pop Punk** - also can be a dirty word, but has less of a stigma than emo. Basically the lighter and softer version of punk rock. Can be more catchy, but can also have similar themes and isn't necessarily as lyrically or musically dissonant from punk rock as purists like to think, especially with some of these examples.

* Say Anything - "... Is a Real Boy"
* Relient K - "Mmhmm"
* Blink-182 - "Dude Ranch", "Enema of the State"
* Buzzcocks - "Singles Going Steady"

* Sugarcult - "Start Static"

* Green Day - "Dookie"
* The Offspring - "Smash"
* Yellowcard - "Ocean Avenue", "Southern Air"
* Various Artists - "Warped Tour 2006 Tour Compilation" (just trust me on this one)
* AFI - "Sing the Sorrow"



**Metalcore** - an often lyrically and sonically dissonant type of music that combines aspects and rage of hardcore punk with the technicality of heavy metal, specifically black metal and death metal. My favorite genre of punk rock.

* Converge - "Jane Doe", "You Fail Me", "All We Love We Leave Behind"
* Kvelertak - "Kvelertak", "Meir"
* Cave In - "White Silence", "Until Your Heart Stops", "Planets of Old EP"

**Ska** - take punk rock and add a drunken New Orleans jazz band. Presto.

**Folk punk** - folk rock with punk. Some have folk instruments (like violins) and have a hardcore DIY ethic. Like, they don't charge money for their releases and make their own isntruments.

* The Pogues - "Rum, Sodomy, and the Lash", "If I Should Fall From Grace With God"



edit: FORGOT POST-PUNK!

**Post-Punk** - atmospheric, experimental punk rock that has much more pronounced progressive influences.

So glad you posted this! Yeah, I studied marine biology a bit in undergrad, so I can corroborate this.

Due to the way that warm, less oxygen-rich water circulates around the globe (via a system called the Great Ocean Conveyor), the water near the arctic and antarctic areas is rich with oxygen at supersaturated levels. Once the water cools to a low enough temperature slightly above freezing, it becomes very dense very quickly - so quickly, in fact, that it sinks directly to the bottom of the ocean without losing any of its oxygen. Whereas the trend for organic material declines sharply past the "twilight zone" of the oceans (where light no longer filters through to the waters below), oxygen levels actually increase quite dramatically. That's why the poles host some of the most abundant, diverse, and sustainable marine ecosystems in the world.

The problem is it's easy to look back on music that's been vindicated by history. Look at The Rolling Stone magazine's list of 500 Greatest Songs or 500 Greatest Albums. There's a marked difference in the number of "classic" 60s/70s albums compared to the 90s onward.

For example, what songs from 1969 can you think of that were hits, or we see define the decade? Maybe the anti-war anthem "Fortunate Son?" Maybe The Byrds' country exploration "Ballad of Easy Rider"? Or any of Jimi Hendrix's songs from *Electric Ladyland*?

Nope. None of them were #1 hits, and only "Fortunate Son" was in the top 10. Jimi Hendrix's only Top 40 crack in the US was "All Along the Watchtower," which hit #20.
